execution.label: Where your code runs
execution.structureNote: Program structure, not an execution trace. Select a stage to inspect its source.
execution.fragmentContract: The lab prepares the inputs, runs your fragment, captures registers and memory, then reports and exits through xv6.
execution.cContract: The supplied caller prepares the arguments, calls lesson, captures the returned state, then reports and exits through xv6.
execution.programContract: xv6 starts your program at _start. Your source supplies its data, initialisation and exit.
execution.fragmentInterval: Stepping starts at your fragment. At its end, the lab captures state and runs the reporter automatically.
execution.cInterval: Stepping starts at lesson. Calls can enter other functions. At the supplied checkpoint, the lab captures state and runs the reporter automatically.
execution.programInterval: Stepping starts at _start. Your program ends when its exit call completes.
execution.dataNote: Program source also shows the data used by your code.
execution.programRouteNote: Your source controls entry and termination. Inspect it to see whether and how the program exits.
execution.fragmentSummary: Supplied setup prepares inputs. Step covers your code; capture, reporting and exit run automatically afterwards.
execution.cSummary: The supplied caller prepares arguments. Step starts at lesson and can enter helpers; capture, reporting and exit follow.
execution.programSummary: Step starts at _start. Your source supplies inputs and data and controls how execution ends.

observation.label: Observed execution
observation.notObserved: Run or start stepping to observe register values.
observation.noPins: Pin registers in Inspect to keep their values here.
observation.captured: Captured after your code, before supplied reporting.
observation.lastPause: Last paused observation. These are not exit register values.
observation.stale: Source changed. These observations belong to the earlier build.
observation.duringRun: Last observation shown. The program is running.
observation.noPausedObservation: Start stepping or Start debugging to observe this program’s registers.

scope.outsideNamed: The last paused PC is in {symbol}, outside this scope.
scope.outsideAddress: The last paused PC, {pc}, is outside this scope.
scope.allMeaning: All changes the listing scope. It does not change where stepping starts or where the supplied capture occurs.
scope.noInstruction: No instruction in this listing matches the last paused PC.

calculator.intro: Scratch work with numbers and bits. It does not run instructions or change the program in the editor.
calculator.width32: Keeps 32 bits. Widening adds upper zeros; narrowing discards upper bits.
calculator.width64: Keeps 64 bits. Selecting 32 bits discards valid values’ upper bits.
calculator.widthIndependence: Calculator width does not change the RV64 processor or the instructions in your program.
calculator.wBridge: RV64 W instructions keep a 32-bit result, then copy bit 31 through the upper 32 positions of a 64-bit register.
calculator.wReading: Signed reading after W sign extension
calculator.sameBits: Signed and unsigned read the same retained bits.
calculator.readingChanged: Decimal reading changed. The retained bits are unchanged; the mathematical reading is updated.
calculator.inputReadingChanged: Decimal reading changed. The input bits are unchanged.
calculator.fullNote: The full mathematical result uses the selected reading of both inputs.
calculator.shiftNote: The full shift result uses A’s unsigned bit pattern. B is a shift amount.
calculator.carryNote: Carries and signed overflow describe the addition. RISC-V does not store arithmetic condition flags.
calculator.wPatternNote: This pattern shows W result formation, calculated from the retained low 32 bits. No CPU instruction was executed.

bridge.title: From a fragment to a complete program
bridge.intro: A fragment uses supplied setup and exit code. A complete program makes those choices in its own source.
bridge.preparationIntro: This example combines memory loads, a helper call and an xv6 exit. Use these lessons if those operations are new.
bridge.workedIntro: The worked program stores two counts in its data section. _start loads them into a0 and a1, then calls combine.
workedDetails: The label _start names the program’s entry. The .data section defines its count values; no Starting setup values are added.
combine puts its result in a0. ret returns to the instruction after the call. The caller copies that value into s0 before using a0 for exit.
The exit request puts zero in a0 and the xv6 exit number in a7. Its ecall enters xv6 to finish the process. This program has no supplied reporter.
workedSteps: Open the worked program as a new project. Your existing project is kept.
Select the line number beside the exit ecall to set a breakpoint. Choose Start debugging.
At that pause, inspect s0 and the data bytes. Explain how each loaded count reached the helper and how the result reached s0.
Choose Continue to let the exit call complete. The retained observations describe the last pause, not the exit state.
bridge.freshTitle: Apply it to a different calculation
bridge.freshTask: The fresh project stores 31 and 17. Change combine to return the first count minus the second. Keep the result in s0 before exit.
bridge.freshPrediction: Predict s0 before running. Set a breakpoint at the exit ecall and inspect the actual observation.
freshQuestions: Which source defines the starting counts, and which instructions load them?
Where does call transfer control, and where does ret return?
Why is the returned result copied before a0 is prepared for exit?
Which pause supports your claimed result, and what does that observation leave unknown about exit?
bridge.success: Check your explanation against the source and paused machine. A matching number alone does not explain the input, call and exit boundaries.
